title: Arthur's Crises

jokes.text: That's something my ex-wife used to tell me.
jokes.setup: Larry's golf partner tells him 'You're supposed to put it in the hole' after a bad shot.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately deflects the golf instruction into a self-deprecating sexual/marital confession about his ex-wife.
jokes.explanation: Classic double-entendre pivot — the golf line works perfectly as an inadvertent setup. The delivery lands because it's both self-deprecating AND economical (six words). It's a familiar move but executed crisply, and it fits Larry's character: narcissistic, neurotic, casually confessional about his failures. Not groundbreaking but well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's something my ex-wife used to tell me.

jokes.text: Card reads: 'To Arthur, the sweetest and... sexiest man in the world.' Cut to: 'To Donna, one of the most beautiful women I've ever had the pleasure to know.'
jokes.setup: The staff is worried about Artie's unprecedented absence at lunch. We see what appears to be a romantic toast card to 'Arthur.'
jokes.punchline: A second card is revealed addressed to Donna — establishing Artie is on a romantic lunch with a woman, which the staff reads as suspicious/professional betrayal.
jokes.explanation: A structurally elegant visual joke: the first card appears to be someone calling Artie 'the sexiest man in the world' (absurd on its face for Rip Torn's gruff character), then the second card reveals he wrote the first one himself in a romantic exchange. The misdirection works on two levels — the content of the cards and the contextual paranoia of the staff. Solid rewatch value because the implication of the affair lands differently once you know the full story.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Artie go out to lunch?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He never goes out to lunch.

jokes.text: And will you give my congratulations and a friendly 'fuck you' to Tom Snyder?
jokes.setup: Artie is chatting warmly about old industry acquaintances — Harry Albertson at CBS, Tom Snyder's move.
jokes.punchline: He pivots from nostalgic warmth to a cheerfully venomous 'friendly fuck you' for Snyder jumping ship, delivered as if it's a perfectly normal pleasantry.
jokes.explanation: The oxymoron 'friendly fuck you' is the whole joke, and it's sharp. Only Artie — the old-school showbiz lifer who can weaponize warmth — delivers this convincingly. The economy is excellent: one phrase does everything. It's funny, it's character-defining, and it's quotable. Not quite legendary but this is exactly the kind of line Rip Torn was born to say.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: When I get stressed out, I retain water. Every year before the emmys, I puff up like a fucking blowfish.

jokes.text: And when I get stressed out, I retain water. Every year before the Emmys, I puff up like a fucking blowfish.
jokes.setup: Beverly is pressing Larry about how many songs Clint Black should perform. She escalates by noting her own stress levels.
jokes.punchline: She catastrophizes her stress into a graphic physical transformation — retaining water and bloating like a blowfish at the Emmys — turning a mundane scheduling question into an absurd personal health crisis.
jokes.explanation: Beverly's oversharing tendency — turning a simple ask into a medical monologue — is good character comedy. The blowfish image is vivid and specific. The Emmy detail contextualizes her vanity nicely. Slightly bloated in delivery (no pun intended) but earns its moment.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Beverly's frantic fan-girl meltdown over Clint Black

jokes.text: Artie's romantic lunch cards revealed — 'Oh, I'm still thinking about last night, Arthur... It was really, really incredible... I was inspired, my dear.'
jokes.setup: The staff is paranoid that Artie may be leaving the show. We see flashback evidence of a lunch.
jokes.punchline: The exchange is clearly romantic and sexual — Artie, the gruff, hard-drinking old TV lifer, is having a passionate affair. The contrast between his persona and 'I was inspired, my dear' is delicious.
jokes.explanation: Extension of the romantic-Artie reveal. The phrase 'I was inspired, my dear' in Rip Torn's gruff voice is inherently funny — it's the incongruity between his weathered persona and the romantic affectation. Works primarily as character comedy and rewatch bonus once you understand the full affair context.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I have to give you a check for the coffee table and the lamp.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: No, sir. I intend to make you work for what you owe.

jokes.text: I have to give you a check for the coffee table and the lamp. / No, sir. I intend to make you work for what you owe. / [suggestive pause and 'Mmmm']
jokes.setup: Artie mentions damage to the hotel room — a broken coffee table and lamp.
jokes.punchline: Donna refuses payment and instead insists he 'work for what he owes' in a clearly sexual context. The implication that their lovemaking destroyed furniture is the hidden escalation.
jokes.explanation: A subtle, well-crafted implication: the furniture destruction establishes the intensity of their encounter without stating it. The comedy is in the gap between polite language ('work for what you owe') and what it clearly means. The 'Mmmm' sells it with economy. This is the Larry Sanders brand of comedy — nothing stated, everything understood.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What are you doing? Now we don't have a lookout. Now, if he comes in, he's gonna see... his calendar.

jokes.text: He's got a hand grenade in here. / What are you doing? Now we don't have a lookout. / Now, if he comes in, he's gonna see... his calendar.
jokes.setup: Staff is snooping in Artie's office, panicking that he'll catch them. One person says 'He's got a hand grenade in here' — building comic tension.
jokes.punchline: The hand grenade turns out to be the setup for a longer beat, but the true anticlimactic punchline is 'he's gonna see... his calendar' — the devastating mundanity of what they're actually afraid of being caught looking at.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of panic (hand grenade!) deflated to 'he'll see his calendar' is excellent deadpan structure. The pause implied before 'his calendar' does a lot of work — it sets up something dramatic and delivers something mundane, which is peak Larry Sanders comedy rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Where is Artie?! Would you keep it down?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You have to speak up, Larry! I can't hear ya!

jokes.text: Yeah. Don Lasner. Guy I went to high school with. He used to hold my head in the urinal and pour Absorbine Junior down my neck.
jokes.setup: Staff is trying to identify 'Dawn Lasner.' Phil says he knows a 'Don Lasner' from high school.
jokes.punchline: Phil's 'Don Lasner' used to torture him in a hilariously specific and grotesque way — holding his head in the urinal and pouring Absorbine Junior (a liniment!) down his neck. The specificity of 'Absorbine Junior' is the joke within the joke.
jokes.explanation: The specific absurdity of 'Absorbine Junior' elevates this from a generic bullying joke to something memorably weird. Absorbine Junior is a horse liniment/muscle rub — why would a bully use that? It's so oddly specific that it feels like a traumatic real memory, which makes it funnier and more disturbing. Phil's matter-of-fact delivery ('Right, that's him. Mystery solved.') treats genuine childhood trauma as trivial, which is the show's comedic signature. The non-sequitur nature and specificity earn this a high craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: First, she steals Snyder. Now she's trying to steal Artie. Fuckers!

jokes.text: 'Right, that's him. Mystery solved. Thanks, Phil.'
jokes.setup: Phil has misidentified Dawn Lasner as the childhood bully 'Don Lasner' who tortured him.
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately dismisses Phil's trauma with 'Right, that's him. Mystery solved. Thanks, Phil' — treating the horrific bullying anecdote as if it conclusively answered the original question.
jokes.explanation: The dismissive straight-man response doubles the joke from #8. The comedy is in the total indifference to Phil's trauma — 'Mystery solved' is a perfect deadpan button. Economy is excellent (four words do all the work). Works as a dependent callback to #8.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: August, I think!

jokes.text: Hank is near-deaf from an air pocket on his flight from Vegas, so all his responses are shouted at the wrong volume, mishearing everything.
jokes.setup: Larry and staff are trying to quietly discuss the sensitive matter of Artie's possible defection.
jokes.punchline: Hank can't hear anything correctly — 'Where is Artie?' becomes a shouted, embarrassing scene; 'Donna Lasner' becomes 'Donna Lasner' (a different mishearing); and 'Don't say anything' becomes 'August, I think!'
jokes.explanation: The deaf Hank running gag is a reliable farce device given new energy by the Vegas air pocket excuse. Hank's character (oblivious, self-absorbed, loud) is perfectly suited to this physical condition. The comedy escalates nicely with each exchange. Not groundbreaking but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: Darlene volunteering to sing with Clint Black

jokes.text: Ha ha. A little bit! / Well, you should see a... doctor. / Never mind. / Last night!
jokes.setup: Larry tries to tell Hank he should see a doctor about his hearing.
jokes.punchline: Hank mishears 'doctor' as something else entirely, Larry gives up mid-sentence ('Never mind'), and Hank's shouted non-sequitur 'Last night!' caps the exchange.
jokes.explanation: The rhythm here is good — Larry's exasperated 'Never mind' mid-sentence is the character comedy; Hank screaming 'Last night!' as a non-sequitur is the absurdist button. Works as part of the sustained gag.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It's great to find some places never change... except for John, the chef. He's dead.

jokes.text: Do you know who Dawn Lasner is? / Donna who?! / Dawn Lasner. Dawn. / Donna Lasner! / No, Dawn.
jokes.setup: Larry tries to whisper 'Dawn Lasner' to Hank as sensitive information.
jokes.punchline: Hank's deafness turns the name into a shouted back-and-forth that defeats the entire purpose of whispering. The name 'Dawn/Donna' confusion escalates the comedy.
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag beat. The Dawn/Donna confusion is a minor wordplay element that serves the farce structure. Not the sharpest beat in the gag but earns its place.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: We split it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, good. Fascinating.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: So we're screwing each other silly. Is that what you want to know about?

jokes.text: He's having lunch with Donna Lasner! She's trying to get him to produce the late-night show after Letterman at 12:30. / Well, not today! / Today!
jokes.setup: Larry explains that Artie is CURRENTLY having lunch with the CBS executive trying to poach him.
jokes.punchline: Hank indignantly declares 'Well, not today!' — mishearing the timing — and Larry corrects him with a defeated 'Today!' The irony of Hank's outrage being directed at the wrong moment.
jokes.explanation: 'Not today!' / 'Today!' is a tight comic exchange — the indignation followed by immediate correction is good timing. Hank's false bravado deflated in one word is character comedy at its most economical.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Ever since I pissed in Larry Tisch's pool on labor day, I've been persona non grata at black rock.

jokes.text: Fuckers! God, don't say anything about this. / What?! / Don't... keep this to yourself! / Oh! / August, I think!
jokes.setup: Larry, furious about Artie's potential defection, tells Hank to keep it quiet.
jokes.punchline: Hank, still deaf, shouts 'What?!' at Larry's hushed plea for secrecy, and then responds to 'keep this to yourself' with the total non-sequitur 'August, I think!' — presumably mishearing something entirely different.
jokes.explanation: 'August, I think!' is the best single beat of the deafness gag — a complete non-sequitur that sounds like a plausible answer to a different question, delivered with Hank's characteristic oblivious confidence. The escalating absurdity of the mishearings peaks here effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You cbs whore.

jokes.text: Darlene crying at Clint Black's sound check — 'It's the music. It's always so sad. I gotta get a camera.'
jokes.setup: Clint Black is doing a melancholy sound check. A staffer mentions that Darlene volunteered to sing with him.
jokes.punchline: Darlene is visibly weeping, explaining 'It's the music. It's always so sad.' The response — 'I gotta get a camera' — treats her emotional breakdown as entertainment.
jokes.explanation: A pleasant character comedy beat — Darlene's operatic emotional response to country music, and the staffer's instinct to document it rather than comfort her. Light and breezy, establishes Darlene's character. Not a standout but works in context.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, no, not if you're riding fence.

jokes.text: He sent me a picture of himself, and he wasn't wearing anything but, uh, like, a small bathing suit... Like a thong? / I don't know. It was just real tiny... Was it running up the crack of his ass? / I didn't check.
jokes.setup: Larry tries to introduce Clint Black to an enthusiastic runner/fan on the show's staff.
jokes.punchline: Clint reveals the fan sent him a photo in a near-thong. Larry's clinical diagnostic questions ('Was it running up the crack of his ass?') transform an awkward celebrity fan situation into an absurd forensic examination of underwear.
jokes.explanation: Larry's pivot from 'help me manage this awkward fan' to 'so was it running up the crack of his ass?' is perfectly in character — he's utterly fixated on the wrong detail, asking increasingly specific questions as if this will resolve something. The exchange has the rhythm of a Seinfeld-ian conversation about nothing important, escalating absurdly. 'I didn't check' from Clint is an excellent deadpan button.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: They'll cut you like a ripe tomato, OK?

jokes.text: Larry venting to Clint Black about disloyalty and people who 'aren't honest' — clearly about Artie — while Clint just asks how many songs he should do.
jokes.setup: Larry pulls Clint aside, supposedly to talk music logistics, but immediately starts venting about betrayal.
jokes.punchline: Clint's genuine question ('How many songs do you think I should do?') cuts right through Larry's self-absorbed monologue, exposing the absurdity of Larry using a celebrity guest as his personal therapist.
jokes.explanation: Larry's narcissism — treating a country music star as a sounding board for his personal drama — is central to the show's comedy. The contrast between Larry's theatrical venting ('not honest, not loyal, all he thinks about is himself') and Clint's practical question ('How about 3?') is perfect. The joke is that Clint barely registers Larry's emotional confession; he just needs to know about the songs.

dialogue.line: Listen, no matter what they tell you, no matter what Larry tells you, they'll cut you like a ripe tomato, OK?

jokes.text: I don't know. How many did Artie say you should do? / Well, I couldn't find him. / He's not around. He's not around. / That's because he's one of those people that I was talking about — not honest, not loyal, all he thinks about is himself.
jokes.setup: Clint asks about Artie's guidance on song count. Larry deferred it as 'Artie's call' earlier.
jokes.punchline: Larry pivots from an honest answer ('He's not here') to immediately prosecuting Artie as a traitor in the same breath — exposing that his earlier professionalism was a mask for paranoid grievance.
jokes.explanation: A dependent joke — only funny in context of the surrounding scene. Larry's inability to separate the professional ('how many songs') from the personal ('he's a traitor') is pure character comedy. Not a standout beat on its own but serves the larger comic sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You must be one hell of a lay.

jokes.text: Dan Tana's. Oh, I haven't been there in 20 years. It's great to find some places never change... except for John, the chef. He's dead.
jokes.setup: Larry casually asks where Artie went for lunch, trying to fish for information.
jokes.punchline: Artie's nostalgic 'great to find some places never change' is immediately undercut by '...except for John, the chef. He's dead.' The non-committal darkness of the afterthought.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The structure is textbook: earnest setup ('great to find some places never change') → exception that destroys the thesis ('except for John, the chef. He's dead.'). The brevity is perfect — 'He's dead' is the entire punchline, delivered with Artie's characteristic matter-of-fact tone. It also works as a dark joke about aging in Hollywood — people and restaurants, some survive, some don't. The character integration is high because only a veteran like Artie casually mentions dead colleagues as a restaurant observation.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm also a good cook, and I mix a stiff drink. Every last one of my wives said they would have divorced me years before, but they just couldn't face life without my herbs and spices.

jokes.text: How's Donna Lasner? / She's fine. / Oh. / Miss Lasner is a dear friend of mine, Larry. / Anything else you want to know? / Nothing. / Sure? / Oh, hey. None of my business.
jokes.setup: Larry has been fishing for information about Artie's lunch. He finally asks directly about Donna Lasner.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Miss Lasner is a dear friend of mine, Larry. Anything else you want to know?' puts Larry on the back foot immediately — a masterclass in stonewalling. Larry's retreat ('Nothing. / Sure? / Oh, hey. None of my business.') is the comedic surrender.
jokes.explanation: The power dynamic reversal — Artie shutting down Larry's interrogation with calm authority — is characteristic of their relationship and very funny. Larry's rapid capitulation ('None of my business') after acting paranoid for ten minutes is perfect character deflation. The rhythm of the exchange ('Nothing. / Sure?') is well-written.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm lying for love.

jokes.text: Ivan, this is where Larry will hold the cards. First gag... Lassie's DNA. / Schwarzenegger's.
jokes.setup: Show prep — they're blocking out card gags for that night's episode.
jokes.punchline: The gag being prepared involves comparing Lassie's DNA to Schwarzenegger's. The absurdity of the content and Larry's exasperated 'Jesus, I'm glad I don't have to do that damn...' (trailing off) implies the bits are ridiculous but he has to do them anyway.
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke about the absurdity of late-night card bits — specifically the kind of hacky DNA/celebrity comparison content that late-night really did air. Larry's revulsion at his own show's material is good self-referential comedy. Slightly underdeveloped — the bit description isn't quite specific enough to fully land.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You didn't just say tough titty, did you?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Tough titty!

jokes.text: So it was just lunch? Nothing else? / Yeah. Kelly! / This chair and the couch, they're off the marks... / Lunch, yes, I had lunch and dessert. / If memory serves, crème brûlée. / Mm-hmm, mm-hmm. / We split it. / Yeah, well, good. Fascinating.
jokes.setup: Larry continues interrogating Artie about the lunch while Artie keeps deflecting with stage management duties.
jokes.punchline: Artie weaponizes mundane detail — describing dessert (crème brûlée, split) in meticulous detail as a way to answer the question while saying nothing. Larry's sarcastic 'Fascinating' is the exasperated straight-man button.
jokes.explanation: Artie's crème brûlée deflection is a good comedy-of-evasion bit. The more specifically mundane he gets ('We split it'), the more it exposes Larry's paranoia as overblown — and the more frustrated Larry becomes. Good character interplay.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Tough titty!

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You didn't just say tough titty, did you?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Tough titty!

jokes.text: So we're screwing each other silly. Is that what you want to know about? / Whew, well, I gotta tell ya. I am relieved. / I thought you were leaving to take that CBS job. / Ha ha! / And you just had an affair! / Oh, sweetheart!
jokes.setup: Larry has been dancing around asking about Artie's relationship with Donna Lasner, clearly terrified he's leaving for CBS.
jokes.punchline: Artie simply states they're having an affair ('screwing each other silly'), and Larry's relief — that it's sex rather than professional betrayal — is immediate and hilariously misplaced. The priorities inversion (an affair = relief) is the heart of the joke.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic and emotional peak — and it earns its high score. The joke is structurally perfect: 10 minutes of building paranoia about professional betrayal pays off with the reveal that it's just a sexual affair, and Larry's reaction ('I am relieved!') perfectly captures his inverted priorities. He would rather his producer destroy a marriage than leave the show. 'And you just had an affair! / Oh, sweetheart!' — Artie's dismissal of Larry's belated moral clarity is perfectly in character. The 'Ha ha!' laugh (Larry's relieved genuine laugh) before the moral recalibration is beautifully written. This is Larry Sanders at its finest: character comedy that is also surprisingly dark.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm afraid I'm going to turn into a lonely old geezer wondering whether your melon got chopped up or whether I told you that your ass isn't fat.

jokes.text: Lunch, yes, I had lunch and dessert. If memory serves, crème brulée. Mm-hmm, mm-hmm, mm-hmm. We split it. Yeah, well, good. Fascinating.
jokes.setup: Larry is clearly angling to ask about Artie and Donna's relationship. Artie provides excruciatingly mundane details about the meal — dessert, what dessert, who paid.
jokes.punchline: Larry's increasingly strained 'Mm-hmm, mm-hmm, mm-hmm. Yeah, well, good. Fascinating.' as Artie plays it completely straight is a masterclass in comedic withholding.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is Artie's total control of the situation — he knows exactly what Larry wants and is making him squirm by answering the wrong version of every question. 'Crème brulée. We split it.' as Larry dies inside is perfectly Larry Sanders. High character integration because this power dynamic between the two is central to the show.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: My ass is fine. My ass is great. I never felt better about my ass.

jokes.text: Ever since I pissed in Larry Tisch's pool on Labor Day, I've been persona non grata at Black Rock.
jokes.setup: Artie explains why he couldn't take the CBS job even if he wanted to — CBS brass would never allow it.
jokes.punchline: The reason for being blacklisted from CBS isn't a professional slight or creative disagreement — it's that he literally urinated in the CBS chairman's pool on a holiday.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's strongest single line. It's absurdly specific (Labor Day, Larry Tisch's pool, 'persona non grata,' 'Black Rock' — the CBS headquarters nickname), it's delivered as if it's a perfectly normal career obstacle, and it reveals everything about Artie's character in one sentence. The joke works on multiple levels: as an industry in-joke (Larry Tisch was the real CBS chairman), as character definition (Artie is the kind of man who does this AND uses 'persona non grata' to describe the aftermath), and as absurdist comedy (the sheer specificity of the humiliation). 'Black Rock' instead of 'CBS' is a perfect writer's-room touch. This is legitimately exceptional television comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Then maybe you and your fat ass can go fuck yourselves.

jokes.text: Larry, Larry, thank you! Thank you! Thank you so much. You're wonderful. I won't let you down. I promise. Thank you! / You OK, Darlene? / I'm wonderful, Artie. Good. / I just have to go throw up now. Thank you.
jokes.setup: Darlene has just been told she can sing with Clint Black — her idol — that night.
jokes.punchline: Her ecstatic gratitude ('You're wonderful. I won't let you down.') immediately followed by 'I just have to go throw up now. Thank you.' The 'Thank you' after announcing she's going to vomit is the button.
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-structured bit of character comedy. The trajectory — overwhelming excitement → immediate nausea — is a classic comedic arc, but the 'Thank you' tacked onto 'I just have to go throw up now' is the detail that elevates it. It's polite, formal, earnest. Darlene's character consistency (she's always a bit much) makes this land.

dialogue.speaker: Wardrobe
dialogue.line: Here's your fucking suit.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Where are the pants?

dialogue.speaker: Wardrobe
dialogue.line: They're letting them out in the butt.

jokes.text: First, I have to throw up again.
jokes.setup: Donna Lasner arrives and Darlene is asked about her wardrobe.
jokes.punchline: Darlene flags that she needs to 'go back to wardrobe' but first, again, must vomit — a callback to her nausea from the excitement.
jokes.explanation: A solid callback — the second vomit mention is funnier for being casual and incidental. 'First, I have to throw up again' treats stage fright nausea as a simple logistical step. Economy is excellent. Weaker than the original beat but pays it off.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You mean the crotch?

jokes.text: Sometimes the staff likes to consult me about their wardrobe each day, something I enjoy taking part in.
jokes.setup: Donna Lasner has just arrived and witnessed the odd spectacle of Darlene asking Larry about her outfit.
jokes.punchline: Larry covers with a transparently false explanation — pretending this is a normal, wholesome management practice rather than his chaotic, boundary-confused workplace.
jokes.explanation: Larry's instinct to manage appearances for CBS — especially for someone potentially stealing his producer — is good character comedy. His spin on workplace dysfunction ('something I enjoy taking part in') is delivered with that particular Larry Sanders earnestness-covering-insecurity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're the happiest we've ever had on the show.

jokes.text: Keep him as long as you like. It's really not a problem... you CBS whore.
jokes.setup: Donna Lasner says she'll only keep Artie a minute. Larry graciously says 'Keep him as long as you like.'
jokes.punchline: Larry's professionalism immediately collapses into 'you CBS whore' the instant Donna is out of earshot (or possibly while she's still there — the blocking ambiguity adds to the cringe).
jokes.explanation: The whiplash from fake graciousness to 'you CBS whore' is executed with perfect economy. Three words after a complete 180 — no setup needed beyond Larry's polite smile. Character integration is extremely high: only Larry Sanders, simultaneously performance-managing his image and imploding with insecurity, says this exact thing this exact way. The word 'whore' applied to network executives is also an industry-insider joke about the morality of network competition. A standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Clint Black
dialogue.line: You just need to find your Lisa.

jokes.text: So it's, you know, out of my hands. I mean, uh, Larry said I was doing 3 songs, and Artie said only one...
jokes.setup: Clint Black is trying to let Darlene down gently about whether she can sing with him — she can't now that Artie has overruled Larry.
jokes.punchline: The comedy is in watching a real country music star awkwardly navigate a TV show's internal politics while a starstruck employee's dreams are being crushed. Clint's 'It's the outfit, isn't it?' / 'Well, no, not if you're riding fence' exchange exposes his discomfort and the absurdity of the situation.
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy — watching Clint awkwardly explain to Darlene that she can't sing. 'It's the outfit, isn't it?' / 'Well, no, not if you're riding fence' is a genuinely funny exchange — Clint's cowboy syntax ('riding fence') is an incongruous detail in a Hollywood TV show context. The sequence is mildly uncomfortable rather than devastating.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I think you're my Lisa, and I think I'm yours.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, jeez! What the fuck!

jokes.text: Kris Kristofferson walks in looking for his pages for tomorrow's sketch, and the staffer gushes that Larry said he's doing 3 songs. Kristofferson: 'Yeah, I think Larry said I'm doing 3 songs.' / Wow! That's great!
jokes.setup: The staffer just watched Clint Black's song count get cut to one due to the Larry/Artie power struggle.
jokes.punchline: Kristofferson, tomorrow's guest, says he's also been told he's doing 3 songs — clearly another case of Larry overpromising. The staffer's 'Wow! That's great!' is hilariously naive given everything we just witnessed with Clint.
jokes.explanation: A smart structural joke — the episode's internal conflict about song count is immediately echoed with tomorrow's guest, implying this chaos is systemic. The staffer's oblivious enthusiasm is good irony. Rewatch bonus for catching the implication that Kristofferson will have the same problem tomorrow.

jokes.text: Hey, I was hearing what you were saying about the 3 songs. Listen, no matter what they tell you, no matter what Larry tells you, they'll cut you like a ripe tomato, OK?
jokes.setup: Hank has overheard Kristofferson mentioning 3 songs and jumps in to warn him.
jokes.punchline: 'They'll cut you like a ripe tomato' — Hank's weirdly specific metaphor for being edited/reduced, delivered with conspiratorial urgency to a confused celebrity guest.
jokes.explanation: 'Cut you like a ripe tomato' is a memorably weird metaphor — specific, slightly non-sensical (a ripe tomato is easy to cut, but that's not a threat?), and delivered with Hank's performative authority. Good character moment for Hank positioning himself as a knowledgeable insider to a celebrity who clearly doesn't know who he is.

jokes.text: I thought I was persona non grata. / Is that right? She offered you the Tom Snyder job. / Yeah. Uh-huh, wow. / You must be one hell of a lay. / I'm also a good cook, and I mix a stiff drink.
jokes.setup: Larry is stunned that Artie was offered the Tom Snyder job at CBS despite being blacklisted (following the Larry Tisch pool incident).
jokes.punchline: Larry's blunt assessment ('You must be one hell of a lay') is met by Artie's proudly expanded self-assessment — he's also a cook and a bartender. The list of domestic/sensual skills as career qualifications is absurdly funny.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed exchange. Larry's 'You must be one hell of a lay' is blunt showbiz cynicism (the only way to overcome a pool-urination blacklist is being great in bed), and Artie's response is perfectly structured — he agrees and then EXPANDS the list of qualifying attributes. 'I mix a stiff drink' delivered with total pride is the cap. Only Artie — old-school, self-assured, sexually confident — pulls this off with dignity rather than sleaziness.

jokes.text: You know, every last one of my wives said they would have divorced me years before, but they just couldn't face life without my herbs and spices.
jokes.setup: Artie is explaining his romantic appeal and domestic skills to Larry.
jokes.punchline: 'Herbs and spices' as the thing keeping multiple wives from leaving — not love, not personality, not fidelity — but culinary skill. The implication that he has had multiple wives who all wanted to leave is the dark undercurrent.
jokes.explanation: This is a near-perfect character joke. 'Herbs and spices' as the glue holding together multiple failed marriages is darkly hilarious — it acknowledges the failure of the marriages implicitly while asserting a bizarre competence as compensation. The phrase 'every last one of my wives' (plural, resigned, matter-of-fact) contains multitudes. Only Artie — seasoned, self-aware, gruff — can say this and make it feel both boastful and tragic. High craft across all dimensions, and extremely quotable.

jokes.text: OK, you and I know I'm not considering it, so calm down. / Well, then what are you doing? Are you lying? / I'm lying for love.
jokes.setup: Larry challenges Artie on why he's 'considering' the CBS offer if he has no intention of taking it.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm lying for love.' — Artie's admission, delivered with complete dignity, that he's fabricating professional interest to protect Donna Lasner's reputation at CBS.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm lying for love' is four words that are both genuinely touching and very funny. The joke is in the dignity — Artie is not ashamed, not sheepish, just matter-of-fact about his romantic pragmatism. It's a beautiful line that works on multiple levels: funny as a confession, funny as a Artie character beat, funny as a contrast to Larry's paranoia. High quotability. Justifies 8.3+.

jokes.text: I'm lying for love. / You're lying for love. / Ohh, I think that's one of the Clint Black songs he's doing tonight. / Well, if it is, it's the only one he'll be singing.
jokes.setup: Artie admits he hasn't turned down the CBS job outright — he's 'lying for love' to protect Donna's feelings.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I think that's one of the Clint Black songs he's doing tonight' repurposes Artie's earnest romantic confession as a country music song title, then Artie undercuts the song count with 'the only one he'll be singing' — a dig at the earlier Clint Black song conflict.
jokes.explanation: A multi-layered callback joke: the phrase 'lying for love' works as a mock country song title, and then Artie's response pivots back to the song count dispute. The structure is elegant — two references compressed into three lines. The final 'the only one he'll be singing' resolves the Clint Black subplot while also serving as Artie asserting his authority ('I cleaned up that mess'). This is writers'-room-level craft.

jokes.text: Well, if it is, it's the only one he'll be singing. I cleaned up that mess. What's the matter with you? 3 songs?
jokes.setup: Artie has returned and discovered that Larry authorized Clint Black to do 3 songs.
jokes.punchline: Artie's indignation at '3 songs' — as if this is an unforgivable creative decision — is funny because it's proportionate to a minor production detail, not the real crisis (his affair, the CBS offer).
jokes.explanation: The '3 songs' running gag payoff — Artie's producer authority reasserting itself. The irony that the emotional crisis gets resolved casually while '3 songs' gets maximum Artie indignation is a nice character observation.

jokes.text: Why don't you just say no? Be done with it for the good of the show. / Hey, buddy. This is my personal area, and you're pushing me. / Now, listen, I just received an offer. Like you do, I'm considering it, and if you can't live with that, Sonny boy... tough titty.
jokes.setup: Larry is pressing Artie to simply reject CBS outright.
jokes.punchline: Artie tells Larry he's overstepping ('This is my personal area'), then delivers a final word: 'tough titty.' The absurd contrast between Artie's dignified old-Hollywood manner and 'tough titty' is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Artie's range — from 'persona non grata' to 'tough titty' in the same episode — is a character comedy feast. 'Tough titty' lands because it's so incongruous with his usual register. 'This is my personal area, and you're pushing me' is also a strong line — territorial, dignified, slightly absurd applied to an emotional conversation.

jokes.text: You didn't just say 'tough titty,' did you? / Tough titty!
jokes.setup: Artie has just said 'tough titty' to Larry's face.
jokes.punchline: Larry's incredulous 'You didn't just say tough titty, did you?' gives Artie the opportunity to repeat it with even more conviction: 'Tough titty!'
jokes.explanation: The repeat escalation of 'Tough titty!' is a classic comedy beat — the incredulous straight man gives the absurdist character the opportunity to double down. Larry's question ('You didn't JUST say...') is perfect because it treats the phrase with such earnest disbelief. Economy is excellent — the entire exchange is five words.

jokes.text: You know what I think? I think you're having a little problem. I think you're afraid that if you say no, she'll dump you.
jokes.setup: Larry is losing the argument with Artie about the CBS offer.
jokes.punchline: Larry's pivot from professional argument to amateur psychoanalysis — diagnosing Artie's real fear as being dumped — is both perceptive and completely out of line. It's a classic Larry Sanders move: emotional accuracy wrapped in inappropriate intrusion.
jokes.explanation: Larry's amateur psychologist routine is a character-defining quirk — he blunders into emotional truths clumsily. The joke works because he's probably right (Artie IS afraid of losing Donna), which makes it more uncomfortable than purely comic. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Aw, that's a crock of horseshit. / I think you're afraid. / Yeah, I'm afraid. / I'm afraid I'm going to turn into a lonely old geezer wondering whether your melon got chopped up or whether I told you that your ass isn't fat. / Too late. / Not for me, buddy. / My ass is fine. My ass is great. I never felt better about my ass.
jokes.setup: Larry has accused Artie of being afraid of losing Donna. Artie denies it, then admits fear — but fear of something completely different.
jokes.punchline: Artie's actual fear is 'turning into a lonely old geezer wondering whether your melon got chopped up' — i.e., becoming an isolated old man worrying about Larry's health. The pivot is unexpected and touching, but the comedy is in the specificity ('your melon got chopped up') and Larry's defensive non-sequitur ('My ass is great. I never felt better about my ass.').
jokes.explanation: This is the emotional and comedic peak of the episode's central relationship. Artie's real fear — becoming a lonely old man worrying about Larry — is revealed in the middle of a comedy argument, delivered with total sincerity before being immediately deflected. 'Your melon got chopped up' as a way of saying 'you die violently' is grotesque and perfect. The topper — Larry's ass defensiveness ('My ass is fine. My ass is great.') pivoting on a word Artie used — is character comedy gold. 'Too late' (Larry admitting his ass is already fat) / 'Not for me, buddy' (Artie refusing to accept the decline) is a beautifully compressed emotional beat. This sequence earns its high score because it's simultaneously funny, earned, and character-defining.

jokes.text: Then maybe you and your fat ass can go fuck yourselves. / Thank you. I was just waiting for a go-ahead. / Go right ahead. Thank you. / Don't wait for me. / I will not wait for you.
jokes.setup: The argument between Artie and Larry has reached its emotional peak — Artie has declared independence.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Thank you. I was just waiting for a go-ahead' treats Artie's furious 'go fuck yourself' as if it's an invitation. The subsequent reciprocal politeness ('Go right ahead. Thank you. / Don't wait for me. / I will not wait for you.') is absurd — they're both being extremely formal while enacting a professional and possibly personal breakup.
jokes.explanation: The escalating formality of a relationship dissolution is executed perfectly. 'Thank you. I was just waiting for a go-ahead' turns 'go fuck yourself' into a polite permission slip — an absurdist reversal. The mirrored 'Don't wait for me / I will not wait for you' is almost Beckettian in its symmetry. The comedy comes from the excessive politeness covering genuine anger and grief.

jokes.text: Hello. / If it means anything to you, Donna, I'm honestly very, very fond of you. / Oh! / I'm not going to stand in the hallway while you try to steal my producer 2 minutes before a show...
jokes.setup: Larry accosts Donna Lasner in the hallway immediately after his blowup with Artie.
jokes.punchline: Larry's opening gambit — 'If it means anything to you, I'm honestly very, very fond of you' to a woman he just called a 'CBS whore' — is hilariously transparent. He then pivots to territorial outrage ('You don't even work here!') before Donna shuts him down.
jokes.explanation: The whiplash from 'CBS whore' to 'I'm honestly very, very fond of you' is the joke — Larry's people-management instinct kicking in despite his true feelings. His speech is simultaneously pompous and pathetic. 'You don't even work here!' as a territorial argument is a lovely Larry Sanders non-sequitur.

jokes.text: Oh, cut the crap, Larry! I'm not taking the job! And I was just leaving.
jokes.setup: Larry has launched into a diplomatically phrased speech about Artie and CBS.
jokes.punchline: Donna cuts right through it — 'Cut the crap, Larry' — revealing the whole confrontation was unnecessary because Artie had already communicated everything. Larry's elaborate approach deflated in six words.
jokes.explanation: The joke is structural: Larry's entire anxious approach (the speech, the 'fond of you' opener) demolished by Donna's brusqueness. The situation turns out to be already resolved, making Larry's intervention simultaneously too late and completely unnecessary — a perfect Larry Sanders beat.

jokes.text: Oh, cut the crap, Larry! I'm not taking the job! And I was just leaving.
jokes.setup: Larry is mid-speech defending his relationship with Artie to Donna.
jokes.punchline: Artie walks in, cuts off Larry's grandstanding in four words, resolves the episode's central conflict, and immediately leaves. All that anxiety, paranoia, and drama — undone by a single declarative sentence.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of deflation — the entire episode's dramatic tension resolved in four words. Only Artie can do this: he's been holding the emotional truth the whole time while everyone around him panicked. 'And I was just leaving' as the kicker is perfect — he's not staying for credit, he's not sentimental about the resolution. Economy score is near-perfect; this is a masterclass in when NOT to explain the joke.

jokes.text: Here's your fucking suit.
jokes.setup: After the emotional resolution of the episode's central conflict, there's a beat — then Artie re-enters.
jokes.punchline: He comes back in just to hand over a suit, with 'Here's your fucking suit.' The mundane task punctuates the dramatic climax; the 'fucking' is a perfect Artie touch — affectionate profanity.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully timed beat. The episode has just had its dramatic peak, and Artie's immediate return to normalcy — delivering a suit — is the comedy. 'Here's your fucking suit' is quintessential Artie: no ceremony, no acknowledgment of the gravity of the previous scene, just practical life continuing. The 'fucking' is not anger — it's affection in Artie's register. Four words, perfect economy, huge character payoff.

jokes.text: Where are the pants? / They're letting them out in the butt. / You mean the crotch?
jokes.setup: Artie delivers Larry's suit. Larry immediately asks about the pants.
jokes.punchline: The pants are being 'let out in the butt' — implying Larry's ass has grown. Larry corrects 'butt' to 'crotch,' implying he'd rather acknowledge one anatomical area expanding than the other. After the previous 'my ass is great' speech, this is a perfect callback.
jokes.explanation: A perfect capper to the ass joke thread. Larry has just loudly defended his ass as 'great' — and now the pants are being let out in the butt. His correction to 'crotch' is a small dignity-preservation move that only makes it worse. Tight, specific, well-timed. Earns big points for callback value.

jokes.text: If you made this decision because you think I can't sing, then you're wrong because I can sing. I can. / ♪ Easier said than done ♪
jokes.setup: Darlene confronts Clint Black about not being able to sing with him tonight.
jokes.punchline: She makes her case — 'I can sing. I can.' — and immediately proves it with an earnest, intimate a cappella performance that is both charming and deeply awkward.
jokes.explanation: The cringe comes from Darlene's total earnestness in an impossible situation. 'I can. I can.' before immediately singing is self-aware comedy — she knows she has to prove it and just goes for it. The awkwardness of an impromptu audition for a celebrity who has already said no is well-executed.

jokes.text: That's... great.
jokes.setup: Darlene has just performed a heartfelt a cappella rendition for Clint Black to prove she can sing.
jokes.punchline: Clint's response — a long pause, then 'That's... great.' — is the sound of a man saying the minimum required to be polite. The ellipsis is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: Two words do all the work. The implied pause before 'great' is the joke — it's the universal sound of someone managing bad news politely. Clint's evident discomfort (a real country star being serenaded by a TV staffer in a hallway) makes this land harder. Economy score is 10 — literally cannot be more economical.

jokes.text: That's... great.
jokes.setup: Darlene has just finished singing to Clint Black in the hallway to prove she can sing.
jokes.punchline: Clint's barely-there 'That's... great.' — the pause before 'great' indicating he had to search for something to say.
jokes.explanation: The pause-before-the-compliment is a classic beat but executed with perfect economy. Clint Black as a straight man is used well here — his celebrity status makes his lukewarm 'That's... great' funnier because he presumably knows what actual singing sounds like.

jokes.text: Hey. Hey, buddy. Come here! / I just want to say good night and, uh, thank you. / Oh, yeah. You're watching me even after the show. I, uh, I don't know if that's a compliment or just, uh, sad. / Heh, probably both.
jokes.setup: Post-show — Larry catches Clint backstage to thank him.
jokes.punchline: Larry's self-deprecating observation that being watched even after the show is 'a compliment or just sad,' and Clint's 'probably both' — a moment of genuine self-awareness from Larry about his own ambivalence toward his success.
jokes.explanation: A small but effective moment of meta-commentary — Larry acknowledging that fandom is both validating and pitiful. Clint's 'probably both' is perfectly calibrated: not cruel, not consoling, just accurate. Character integration is good for Larry (this kind of existential self-deprecation is his mode).

jokes.text: Well, uh, you know, I got married, and, uh, my wife, you know, brought balance to my life, and, uh, smoothed out all the bumps, you know. You just need to find your Lisa.
jokes.setup: Larry marvels that Clint seems so happy and grounded. Clint explains it's his wife.
jokes.punchline: Clint says 'You just need to find your Lisa' — a sincere, if slightly clichéd piece of relationship advice — which lands as unintentionally absurd given everything we know about Larry's romantic history and character.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is structural — 'find your Lisa' is generic celebrity advice that means nothing in Larry's context. The dramatic irony is that the audience knows Larry is constitutionally incapable of this. Sets up the final joke perfectly.

jokes.text: Ohhh. / Fuckin' beautiful. Have a drink.
jokes.setup: Clint has told Larry he just needs to 'find his Lisa.' Larry is visibly moved.
jokes.punchline: Artie's response to the earnest romantic advice — 'Fuckin' beautiful' — is perfectly calibrated Artie: genuine appreciation expressed in profanity, immediately followed by a drink invitation that is itself an act of masculine intimacy.
jokes.explanation: 'Fuckin' beautiful' as genuine appreciation is a signature Artie register — he expresses tenderness through profanity. 'Have a drink' is both a deflection and an invitation. The character integration is very high.

jokes.text: I just started to realize something that's a little scary. / Yeah. Try me. / I think you're my Lisa, and I think I'm yours. / Oh, jeez! What the fuck!
jokes.setup: After Clint Black leaves, having said Larry 'just needs to find his Lisa,' Larry has an epiphany.
jokes.punchline: Larry tells Artie: 'I think you're my Lisa, and I think I'm yours.' He has mapped their professional codependency onto a romantic framework. Artie's horrified 'Oh, jeez! What the fuck!' is the episode's final beat — and it perfectly captures both men: Larry's need for emotional connection and Artie's absolute refusal to acknowledge it in those terms.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's masterpiece joke, and it earns all its scores. The entire episode has been about the Larry-Artie relationship — Artie's potential departure, Larry's panic, Artie's real fear of lonely old age watching out for Larry, their argument and reconciliation. The Clint Black 'find your Lisa' scene sets up the final beat perfectly. Larry's declaration that Artie IS his Lisa — his romantic/emotional soulmate analog — is simultaneously hilarious, touching, and perfectly true. It reframes the entire episode as a love story between two men who would never use that language. Artie's 'Oh, jeez! What the fuck!' is the perfect response: horrified, but not leaving. The structure is impeccable — everything in the episode has been a setup for this punchline. Character integration is off the charts: no other show, no other characters could land this exact joke this way.

jokes.text: I'll tell ya something. I just started to realize something that's a little scary. / Yeah. Try me. / I think you're my Lisa, and I think I'm yours. / Oh, jeez! What the fuck!
jokes.setup: Inspired by Clint's speech about finding his 'Lisa,' Larry turns to Artie — who just had the fight of their relationship — with something to say.
jokes.punchline: 'I think you're my Lisa, and I think I'm yours.' The declaration of emotional co-dependence between two heterosexual men in showbiz, coming immediately after their massive fight. Artie's 'Oh, jeez! What the fuck!' is the perfect response.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and one of the finest closers the show has done. The structure is perfect: the entire episode has been about Larry's fear of losing Artie, and Clint's speech about 'finding your Lisa' provides the language for what Larry and Artie are to each other. The callback is earned because the whole episode has been building toward the acknowledgment that their relationship IS the show's love story. Larry saying it is funny because it's both absolutely true and completely inappropriate/oversharing in a masculine showbiz context. Artie's 'Oh, jeez! What the fuck!' is the ideal response — not denial, not warmth, just visceral bewilderment that someone named the thing. This earns its 8+ score because: (1) it's a perfect structural callback, (2) it's character-irreplaceable, (3) it has genuine emotional weight that makes it funnier, and (4) Artie's response is the perfect button. High quotability because the line is memorable and context-free quotable.

tmdb_overview: Larry fears that Artie's intimate relationship with a CBS network executive spells the end of their relationship. Darlene longs to sing with Clint Black.
